 Mandatory Automatic Enrollment Under SECURE 2.0: A Technical Analysis of Treasury Decision 10061 and the Final Section 414A Regulations 
 November 17, 2026 
 by Ed Zollars, CPA 
 Treasury Decision 10061 (RIN 1545-BR08), November 18, 2026
 The enactment of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 (Division T of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, Public Law 117-328) fundamentally altered the statutory framework governing employer-sponsored defined contribution plans. Chief among its structural reforms is Section 101 of the Act, which codified Internal Revenue Code (Code) Section 414A. For decades, automatic contribution arrangements functioned as voluntary, design-based safe harbors under Code Sections 401(k)(13) and 414(w), enacted by the Pension Protection Act of 2006 (Public Law 109-280). Code Section 414A transforms automatic enrollment from an elective feature into an affirmative qualification requirement for new cash or deferred arrangements (CODAs) and Section 403(b) salary reduction agreements.
 On November 18, 2026, the Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) published Treasury Decision 10061 (RIN 1545-BR08), issuing final regulations under Code Section 414A (Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1) and promulgating conforming amendments to the eligible automatic contribution arrangement (EACA) regulations under Code Section 414(w) (Treas. Reg. § 1.414(w)-1). For certified public accountants, enrolled agents, and employee benefits practitioners, TD 10061 provides long-awaited administrative finality regarding coverage mandates, statutory escalation mechanics, investment safe harbors, corporate transaction rules, and grandfathering exemptions.
 This analysis provides a comprehensive examination of the final regulations, detailing Treasury’s statutory justification, structural additions and deletions to existing regulations, modifications made to the proposed regulations, the IRS’s legal analysis addressing public comments, and the bifurcated effective and applicability date framework.
 Statutory Authority and Impetus for Regulatory Promulgation 
 Treasury promulgated these final regulations pursuant to its general rulemaking authority under Code Section 7805(a), which empowers the Secretary to “prescribe all needful rules and regulations for the enforcement of [the Code], including all rules and regulations as may be necessary by reason of any alteration of law in relation to internal revenue.” In addition, statutory authority is grounded in Section 341 of the SECURE 2.0 Act, which directs the Secretaries of the Treasury and Labor to issue regulations governing the consolidation of employee benefit plan notices.
 In its regulatory impact analysis under Executive Orders 12866 and 13563, Treasury articulated the fundamental administrative need for regulatory intervention:
 “The regulations are necessary because section 101 of the SECURE 2.0 Act sets out the broad rule that certain new 401(k) and 403(b) plans must use automatic enrollment but does not provide the required operational details. The regulations provide guidance on exactly who must be covered, how to calculate and increase default contribution rates, when an escalation schedule can be reset, how the investment default rules apply, and how statutory exceptions (such as for pre-enactment plans, plans maintained by new businesses, and plans maintained by small businesses) work.”
 Prior to this rulemaking, the IRS issued interim guidance in Notice 2024-2 (2024-2 I.R.B. 316), offering preliminary question-and-answer guidance on Code Section 414A. Subsequently, on January 14, 2025, Treasury released a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (REG-100669-24, 90 FR 3092). Following an extensive public comment process involving eighteen formal submissions and a public hearing held on April 8, 2025, Treasury finalized the regulatory package in TD 10061.
 Treasury and the IRS underscored that the economic stakes of these operational rules are substantial. Actuarial and economic models cited in the preamble estimate that Code Section 414A will increase retirement savings by $4.2 billion annually on average between 2023 and 2032, affecting approximately 2.2 million taxpayers and 31,600 retirement plans each year. Treasury projects an overall 7 percentage point increase in participation rates (from 70 percent to 77 percent) in affected plans, with roughly 50 percent of covered employees remaining at default contribution rates.
 Structural Additions and Deletions in the Final Regulations 
 Treasury Decision 10061 implements permanent structural additions to Title 26 of the Code of Federal Regulations, establishing Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1 while amending existing Treas. Reg. § 1.414(w)-1 and Part 602.
 Promulgation of Treasury Regulation Section 1.414A-1 
 The core substantive framework is codified at Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1, organized into six operational subsections:
 Paragraph (a) (Overview): Outlines the scope of the regulation and the statutory interplay between plan qualification and the automatic contribution mandate. 
 Paragraph (b) (General Rule): Imposes the core qualification condition. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(b)(1), a CODA will fail to be treated as a qualified CODA under Code Section 401(k) and Treas. Reg. § 1.401(k)-1(a)(4)(i) unless any cash or deferred election satisfies the automatic enrollment rules of paragraph (c). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(b)(2), a salary reduction agreement under a Section 403(b) plan will fail to be treated as purchased under a Section 403(b) annuity contract under Treas. Reg. § 31.3121(a)(5)-2(a)(1) unless it complies with paragraph (c). 
 Paragraph (c) (Automatic Enrollment Requirements): Details the substantive standards governing covered employees, mandatory permissible withdrawals under Code Section 414(w)(2), uniform initial percentages, annual automatic escalation, permissive initial period redeterminations, and default investment compliance. 
 Paragraph (d) (Plan and Business Exceptions): Establishes the operational parameters for statutory exemptions, including SIMPLE 401(k) plans under Code Section 401(k)(11), governmental plans under Code Section 414(d), church plans under Code Section 414(e), new businesses in existence for less than three years, and small businesses normally employing ten or fewer employees. 
 Paragraph (e) (Pre-Enactment Grandfathering and Mergers): Formulates the grandfathering exception for CODAs and Section 403(b) plans established prior to December 29, 2022, providing precise governance rules for plan mergers, spin-offs, multiple employer plans (MEPs), and subsequent plan amendments. 
 Paragraph (f) (Applicability Dates): Sets forth the statutory applicability date, the regulatory applicability date, and the transitional good-faith compliance standard.
 Amendments and Deletions Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.414(w)-1 
 Under the prior regulatory regime established by TD 9447 (74 FR 8200, Feb. 24, 2009), an EACA was an elective arrangement that afforded employers relief from statutory distribution restrictions to permit 90-day unwinding distributions (permissible withdrawals). Crucially, under former Treas. Reg. § 1.414(w)-1(b)(1), an EACA was permitted to cover a selectively designated subset of employees (such as newly hired employees only).
 TD 10061 deletes this discretionary flexibility for plans subject to Code Section 414A by revising the second sentence of Treas. Reg. § 1.414(w)-1(b)(1) to read:
 “Except to the extent required under section 414A (which applies to plan years beginning after December 31, 2024), an eligible automatic contribution arrangement need not cover all employees who are eligible to elect to have contributions made on their behalf under the applicable employer plan.”
 Consequently, for any plan governed by Code Section 414A, an EACA can no longer be limited to new cohorts; it must cover all eligible employees under the CODA or salary reduction agreement.
 In addition, TD 10061 amends Treas. Reg. § 1.414(w)-1 by adding paragraph (b)(4), which introduces two vital administrative safe harbors:
 Exemption for Unenrolled Participants (Treas. Reg. § 1.414(w)-1(b)(4)(i)): Implements Code Section 414(bb) (added by Section 320 of the SECURE 2.0 Act). It relieves plan administrators from the obligation to furnish the annual EACA notice required by Code Section 414(w)(4) and Treas. Reg. § 1.414(w)-1(b)(3) to an “unenrolled participant” (as defined in Code Section 414(bb)(2)), provided the participant receives an annual reminder notice under Code Section 414(bb)(1)(A) and ERISA Section 111(c), along with any plan documents requested. 
 Consolidation of Plan Notices (Treas. Reg. § 1.414(w)-1(b)(4)(ii)): Formulates a unified five-prong standard under Section 341 of the SECURE 2.0 Act, permitting the EACA notice to be combined into a single disclosure document with notices required under ERISA Sections 404(c)(5)(B) (QDIA), 514(e)(3) (ERISA preemption), 801(d)(3)(A) (pension-linked emergency savings accounts or PLESAs), and Code Sections 401(k)(12)(D) (traditional safe harbor) or 401(k)(13)(E) (QACA safe harbor). The combined notice must: 
 Include the required statutory content; 
 Clearly identify the issues addressed therein; 
 Be furnished at the time and frequency required for each constituent notice; 
 Be presented in a manner reasonably calculated to be understood by the average plan participant; and 
 Not obscure or fail to highlight the primary information required for each notice.
 Finally, conforming amendments were made to 26 CFR Part 602, updating the table in Treas. Reg. § 602.101(b) to display OMB Control Number 1545-2135 for both Treas. Reg. §§ 1.414(w)-1 and 1.414A-1.
 Substantive Revisions from Proposed to Final Regulations 
 Treasury adopted the proposed regulations with several critical technical modifications in direct response to public comments submitted by the employee benefits bar and plan sponsor community.
 Flexibility in Timing and Magnitude of Automatic Escalation 
 Under proposed Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(c)(3)(ii)(B), a plan was required, for each plan year beginning after an employee’s initial period, to increase the default contribution rate by exactly one percentage point on the first day of the plan year until reaching at least 10 percent. Commenters urged Treasury to permit plan sponsors to apply the automatic increase on dates other than the first day of the plan year (for example, aligning escalation with an employer’s fiscal compensation review date) and to allow annual escalations exceeding one percentage point.
 Treasury adopted this recommendation in Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(c)(3)(ii)(B), restructuring the escalation requirement:
 “In response to the comments, §1.414A-1(c)(3)(ii)(B) clarifies the language of the proposed regulation by providing that, not later than the first day of each plan year beginning after an employee’s initial period, the percentage contribution under the default election applicable to the employee on the first day of the prior plan year must be increased by at least one percentage point. This clarification allows for flexibility in the timing and amount of the increase. The final regulation also provides that annual increases must occur until the employee’s percentage contribution is at least 10 percent. Under the final regulation, a plan may provide that the annual increases continue after the employee’s percentage contribution is 10 percent but may not provide for the annual increases to continue after the employee’s percentage contribution is equal to 15 percent.”
 This modification affords plan sponsors operational flexibility: an employer may escalate default deferrals prior to the first day of the plan year, and may accelerate escalation by applying two or three percentage points annually, provided the statutory minimums are satisfied and the 15 percent ceiling is not breached.
 Limitation of Default Investment Rules to Participant-Directed Plans 
 Code Section 414A(b)(4) dictates that default contributions for which no participant investment election is made must be invested in accordance with Department of Labor (DOL) qualified default investment alternative (QDIA) regulations under 29 CFR § 2550.404c-5. Commenters pointed out that proposed Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(c)(4) appeared to impose this QDIA mandate across all plans, even though certain defined contribution plans maintain trustee-directed investments with no individual participant investment direction.
 Treasury amended Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(c)(4) to restrict the scope of the investment mandate. As finalized:
 “In response to the comments, §1.414A-1(c)(4) provides that the requirements of 29 CFR 2550.404c-5 (or any successor regulations) apply to amounts contributed pursuant to an EACA only if the EACA is part of a plan that offers an employee the opportunity to direct the investment of all or a portion of the assets allocated to the employee’s individual account under the plan. This is consistent with section 414A(b)(4), under which the requirements of 29 CFR 2550.404c-5 (or any successor regulations) apply if the employee chooses not to make an investment election. Section 1.414A-1(c)(4) also clarifies that the requirements of 29 CFR 2550.404c-5 (or any successor regulations) apply to amounts contributed pursuant to an EACA only if the EACA is part of a plan that is subject to title I of ERISA.”
 Consequently, non-participant-directed plans and plans outside Title I of ERISA are relieved from the QDIA requirements under Section 414A(b)(4).
 Incorporation of Predecessor Employer Standard for New Businesses 
 Code Section 414A(c)(4)(A) exempts a qualified CODA or Section 403(b) plan while the employer maintaining the plan “(and any predecessor employer) has been in existence for less than 3 years.” The proposed regulations reserved on the definition of “predecessor employer.” In response to comments requesting objective criteria, particularly in the context of mergers and asset acquisitions, Treasury adopted Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(d)(4)(i), explicitly linking the definition to the existing standard under Treas. Reg. § 1.415(f)-1(c):
 “In response to these comments, §1.414A-1(d)(4)(i) provides that, for purposes of the new business exception, a predecessor employer is a predecessor employer within the meaning of §1.415(f)-1(c). Thus, the final regulation includes a definition of predecessor employer in the situation in which a plan is maintained by a successor as well as a situation in which a plan is not maintained by a successor.”
 Controlled Group and Affiliated Service Group Aggregation Rules 
 Addressing ambiguity in the proposed regulations regarding whether the new business (less than 3 years) and small business (normally employs 10 or fewer employees) exceptions evaluate headcounts on a single-entity or aggregated basis, Treasury added Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(d)(4)(iv). The final rule establishes that for non-multiple employer plans:
 “the term employer includes all members of a group of employers that are treated as a single employer under the rules of section 414(b), (c), (m), or (o).”
 For multiple employer plans (MEPs), the final regulation clarifies that the term employer includes all employers treated as a single employer under Treas. Reg. § 1.413-2(a)(2)(ii). Furthermore, pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(d)(4)(iii), new and small business exceptions apply on an employer-by-employer basis within a MEP.
 Formalities for Ongoing Plan Designation in Corporate Mergers 
 Under proposed Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(e)(3)(ii), if a pre-enactment grandfathered plan merges with a post-enactment non-grandfathered plan in connection with an asset or stock acquisition or merger described in Treas. Reg. § 1.410(b)-2(f), the merged plan retains its pre-enactment exemption only if the pre-enactment plan is designated as the ongoing plan and the merger occurs within the transition period under Code Section 410(b)(6)(C)(ii). Commenters requested that Treasury dispense with the requirement to designate the pre-enactment plan as the ongoing plan, or clarify that the designation does not have to appear in the formal plan document.
 Treasury retained the ongoing plan designation requirement in Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(e)(3)(ii)(B), but provided significant administrative relief in the preamble:
 “Section 1.414A-1(e)(3)(ii)(B) retains the condition in the proposed regulation requiring that the pre-merger pre-enactment plan be designated as the ongoing plan. However, the Treasury Department and the IRS agree with the commenter that the designation of an ongoing plan under §1.414A-1(e)(3)(ii)(B) should be documented in writing but does not need to be in the written plan document.”
 This confirms that contemporaneous corporate resolutions, merger agreements, or written administrative minutes satisfy the designation condition.
 Delayed Regulatory Applicability Date and Pre-414A Employee Transition Mechanics 
 The proposed regulations contemplated an applicability date for plan years beginning more than six months following publication of the final rule. Commenters demonstrated that plan administrators, third-party recordkeepers, and payroll software vendors required substantial lead time to reprogram auto-escalation algorithms and notice delivery systems.
 In response, Treasury delayed the regulatory applicability date in Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(f)(2) to plan years beginning after December 31, 2027, while establishing that for prior plan years (beginning after December 31, 2024), a reasonable, good faith interpretation standard governs.
 Furthermore, Treasury introduced a vital transitional rule in the preamble addressing “pre-414A employees.” Under Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(c)(1)(ii), an EACA must cover all employees eligible to make deferrals, including those eligible prior to the statutory applicability date. For a calendar year plan, Code Section 414A statutorily applied on January 1, 2025. For an employee eligible prior to 2025 who was not enrolled under the EACA, the statutory initial period under Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(c)(3)(ii)(A) commenced January 1, 2025, and concluded on the last day of the following plan year—December 31, 2026. Because this initial period expires before the regulatory applicability date (January 1, 2028), the preamble to TD 10061 provides plan sponsors with a permissive redetermination choice:
 “For a pre-414A employee who, under the final regulation, must be automatically enrolled as of the first day of the 2028 plan year, the plan terms could permit a redetermination of the initial period for the pre-414A employee. This redetermination is similar to the initial-period redetermination permitted in the final regulation for an employee who did not have default elective contributions made for an entire plan year, and it is permitted even though the pre-414A employee did not make an affirmative election. Thus, the plan is permitted to provide that the default contribution percentage that applies to the pre-414A employee is the percentage that would have applied under the EACA if the initial period for the pre-414A employee had started on the first day of the 2028 plan year. In the alternative, the plan is permitted to provide that the default contribution percentage that applies to the pre-414A employee is the percentage that would have applied under the EACA for the 2028 plan year had the pre-414A employee been covered by the EACA starting on the first day of the 2025 plan year.”
 Treasury and IRS Legal Analysis Justifying Regulatory Positions 
 In TD 10061, Treasury and the IRS conducted an exacting statutory analysis, rejecting numerous commenter requests for administrative exemptions where such carve-outs lacked grounding in the text of Code Section 414A.
 Universal Coverage Mandate and Rejection of Employee-Category Exclusions 
 Multiple commenters requested that final regulations permit employers to exclude specific employee cohorts from the mandatory EACA, specifically advocating for the exclusion of collectively bargained employees and existing employees who were eligible prior to the plan becoming subject to Section 414A.
 Treasury flatly rejected these requests, grounding its determination in the strict textual boundaries of the statute:
 “Although section 414A(c) provides several exceptions to the requirements of section 414A(a) for certain types of plans, no provision in section 414A (or in section 101(c) of the SECURE 2.0 Act) excludes any category of employee from the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A(b) of the Code if the plan is subject to section 414A(a). Accordingly, §1.414A-1(c)(1)(ii) retains the rule from the proposed regulation and clarifies that each employee who is eligible to elect to have contributions made on the employee’s behalf under a CODA or pursuant to a salary reduction agreement must be covered by the EACA, which includes an employee who was eligible to participate in the CODA or salary reduction agreement before the CODA or salary reduction agreement became subject to the automatic enrollment requirements of section 414A(b).”
 The only exception sanctioned by the statute is found in Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(c)(1)(iii), which protects an employee who has an affirmative election currently in effect (to contribute a specified percentage or dollar amount, or affirmatively electing zero contributions) on the date Section 414A first applies to the plan.
 Long-Term, Part-Time Employees 
 Commenters requested special timing flexibility for automatically enrolling long-term, part-time (LTPT) employees eligible under Code Section 401(k)(2)(D). Treasury declined to create specialized rules, confirming that the standard EACA notice timing rules under Treas. Reg. § 1.414(w)-1(b)(3)(iii) (notice 30 to 90 days prior to the plan year, or within a reasonable period prior to initial eligibility) and the election timing requirements of Treas. Reg. § 1.414(w)-1(e)(2) govern LTPT employees without alteration.
 Preservation of Full Plan Year Requirement for Initial Period Resets 
 Under Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(c)(3)(iv), a plan is permitted to redetermine an employee’s initial period if the employee experiences an entire plan year without default elective contributions. Paragraph (c)(3)(iv)(B) permits a reset for a rehired employee who had no contributions because the employee was ineligible for an entire plan year, setting a new initial period beginning when the employee is re-eligible. Paragraph (c)(3)(iv)(C) permits a reset where an employee made an affirmative election (such as opting out) that remained in effect for an entire plan year, permitting the plan to re-apply default auto-escalation at a future date specified by the plan (e.g., an annual re-enrollment sweep).
 Commenters requested that the IRS eliminate the requirement that an employee be ineligible for an entire plan year, or permit resets for rehired employees who were separated for less than a full year. The IRS rejected the request, explaining its legal and structural rationale:
 “Section 1.414A-1(c)(3)(iv) retains the requirement of the proposed regulation requiring an entire plan year of ineligibility or an entire plan year of contributions made pursuant to an affirmative election, regardless of whether the affirmative election contribution percentage is less than the default percentage, before the plan can implement the initial default percentage by redetermining the rehired employee’s initial period. This language is intended to parallel, not modify, the rules currently applicable to a QACA under §1.401(k)-3(j)(2)(iv), which states that for purposes of determining the date the initial period begins, a plan is permitted to treat an employee who for an entire plan year did not have contributions made pursuant to a default election under the QACA as if the employee had not had such contributions made for any prior plan year as well. In addition, the final regulation balances the requirement of automatic increases at regular intervals with concerns regarding the administrative feasibility of determining an individual’s default contribution percentage based on older data.”
 Small Business Counting Rules and Permanent Cessation of Exemption 
 Code Section 414A(c)(4)(B) provides that automatic enrollment does not apply to a plan earlier than the date that is one year after the close of the first taxable year with respect to which the employer maintaining the plan “normally employed more than 10 employees.”
 In response to comments advocating for employee counting methods derived from SIMPLE IRAs or the small employer pension startup credit under Code Section 45E, Treasury insisted upon using the COBRA counting regulations:
 “However, because the phrase normally employed is used in section 4980B(d)(1) and Q&A-5 of §54.4980B-2 but not in section 45E, §1.414A-1(d)(4)(ii) retains the rule from the proposed regulation providing that the number of employees that the employer normally employs for a taxable year is determined using the rules of Q&A-5 of §54.4980B-2 and does not permit the alternative requested by the commenter.”
 Under Treas. Reg. § 54.4980B-2, Q&A-5, an employer is treated as normally employing more than 10 employees if it employed more than 10 employees on at least 50 percent of its typical business days during the preceding calendar year.
 Addressing whether an employer that drops back down to 10 or fewer employees regains the exemption, Treasury confirmed the permanent “once out, always out” rule:
 “Section 1.414A-1(d)(4)(ii) retains the language of the proposed regulation. Thus, the requirements of §1.414A-1(b) do not apply before the first plan year that begins at least 12 months after the close of the first taxable year of the employer maintaining the plan with respect to which that employer normally employed more than 10 employees. The Treasury Department and the IRS agree with the first commenter’s interpretation that the requirements of §1.414A-1(b) continue to apply for subsequent plan years even if the employer no longer normally employs more than 10 employees, including in the case of a corporate event.”
 Pre-Enactment Status for Multiemployer Plans 
 Addressing Code Section 414A(c)(2)(A), commenters questioned whether a multiemployer defined benefit or pension plan in existence prior to December 29, 2022, could adopt a new 401(k) CODA post-enactment and claim grandfathered status. The IRS strictly parsed the statutory language:
 “Section 1.414A-1(e)(1)(i) retains the rule from the proposed regulation. This rule reflects section 414A(c)(2)(A)(i) and applies to multiemployer plans. Therefore, a multiemployer plan qualifies for the exception from the requirements of section 414A only if plan terms were adopted providing for the qualified CODA before December 29, 2022. If they were not, then the plan would not qualify for the exception.”
 Treasury noted that under Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(e)(1)(i), pre-enactment status is determined by the adoption date of the plan terms providing for the CODA, even if the effective date of the CODA was subsequent to December 29, 2022.
 Mergers and Statutory Transition Periods 
 Under Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(e)(3)(ii)(C), when a non-grandfathered plan merges into a grandfathered pre-enactment single-employer plan following a corporate transaction under Treas. Reg. § 1.410(b)-2(f), the merged plan retains pre-enactment grandfathering only if the merger occurs within the transition period described in Code Section 410(b)(6)(C)(ii) (ending on the last day of the first plan year beginning after the date of the ownership change). Commenters requested extending this merger window by an additional eighteen months. Treasury rejected this modification:
 “Section 410(b)(6)(C)(ii) provides a period for an employer to implement changes to its plans that may be needed following a transaction described in section 410(b)(6)(C). The Treasury Department and the IRS believe that this transition period is sufficient for an employer to implement a plan merger to preserve a plan’s pre-enactment status under section 414A. Accordingly, §1.414A-1(e)(3)(ii)(C) retains the condition in the proposed regulation that the plan merger occur within the transition period described in section 410(b)(6)(C)(ii).”
 Cross-Employer Deferral Election Portability 
 Commenters requested that Treasury create an exception to the uniform percentage requirement allowing an employee’s deferral election from a prior employer’s 401(k) or 403(b) plan to carry over to a new, unrelated employer’s plan. Treasury declined, expressing privacy and structural objections:
 “The Treasury Department and the IRS have concerns about the complexity of, and disclosure concerns inherent in, allowing for elections under one plan to be taken into account under another unrelated plan without an individual providing consent.”
 Interaction with Pension-Linked Emergency Savings Accounts 
 Addressing PLESAs authorized under Code Section 402A(e), Treasury noted that an affirmative election to contribute to a PLESA constitutes an affirmative election under the CODA. However, Treasury affirmed that automatic enrollment into a PLESA cannot be utilized to satisfy Code Section 414A:
 “If an employee is automatically enrolled to contribute to a PLESA, the investment requirements of section 414A(b)(4) and proposed §1.414A-1(c)(4) (which reference the Department of Labor’s rules for QDIAs under 29 CFR 2550.404c-5) generally would not be satisfied with respect to the automatic contributions to the PLESA... Thus, automatic contributions to the PLESA would not be able to be used to satisfy the automatic enrollment requirements under section 414A.”
 Because statutory PLESA provisions require capital preservation investments (such as cash or interest-bearing accounts), they inherently conflict with DOL QDIA regulations (such as target-date funds), precluding dual compliance.
 Distinction Between QACA Safe Harbor and Section 414A Compliance 
 Finally, Treasury rejected the argument that satisfying QACA safe harbor rules under Code Section 401(k)(13) and Treas. Reg. § 1.401(k)-3(j) automatically satisfies Code Section 414A:
 “The Treasury Department and the IRS do not agree. The requirements under section 414A and the rules under section 401(k)(13) are separate, and the requirements under section 414A apply in addition to any rules under section 401(k)(13). Section 414A includes requirements that are not found in section 401(k)(13) and §1.401(k)-3(j) and (k), including the requirement in section 414A(b)(2) that the arrangement be an eligible automatic contribution arrangement that allows employees to make permissible withdrawals (as defined in section 414(w)(2)) and the requirement in section 414A(b)(4) that certain amounts contributed pursuant to the arrangement be invested in accordance with the requirements of 29 CFR 2550.404c-5 (or any successor regulations).”
 Treasury also highlighted that the definition of the “initial period” differs between the two regimes. Under QACA regulations (Treas. Reg. § 1.401(k)-3(j)(2)(ii)(A)), the initial period commences when an employee first has default contributions made. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(c)(3)(ii)(A)(2), the initial period begins on the date the employee is first eligible to make an election under the plan (or, if later, when Section 414A first applies to the plan). While plans can be drafted to comply harmoniously with both rules, Section 414A imposes distinct legal obligations.
 Effective and Applicability Dates with Transition Rules for Plan Sponsors 
 Practitioners must carefully advise plan sponsor clients regarding the multi-tiered effective date structure established in TD 10061:
 Federal Register Effective Date: The formal effective date of Treasury Decision 10061 is sixty days following its publication in the Federal Register (January 19, 2027). 
 Statutory Applicability Date: Pursuant to Section 101(c) of the SECURE 2.0 Act, Code Section 414A applies statutorily to plan years beginning after December 31, 2024. 
 Regulatory Applicability Date: Under Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(f)(2) and amended Treas. Reg. § 1.414(w)-1, the final regulations formally apply to plan years beginning after December 31, 2027 (calendar year 2028 for calendar-year plans). 
 Interim Reasonable Good Faith Compliance: For plan years beginning after December 31, 2024, but prior to the regulatory applicability date (e.g., the 2025, 2026, and 2027 plan years), Treas. Reg. § 1.414A-1(f)(2) provides that:
 “For prior plan years, a reasonable, good faith interpretation standard applies with respect to section 414A.”
 Compliance with the proposed regulations (REG-100669-24), Notice 2024-2, or these final regulations is deemed to satisfy the reasonable, good faith interpretation standard during this transition window.
 Practitioner Action Plan and Compliance Takeaways 
 To ensure that employer plans maintain qualified status and avoid inadvertent operational failures that would jeopardize tax-favored treatment under Code Sections 401(a) and 403(b), CPAs and EAs should execute the following compliance actions:
 Review Plan Inception Dates and Controlled Group Structures: Review plan establishment documentation to verify whether CODAs were adopted prior to December 29, 2022. For employers relying on new business or small business exemptions, perform annual controlled group and affiliated service group headcounts under Code Sections 414(b), (c), (m), and (o) utilizing the COBRA counting standard in Treas. Reg. § 54.4980B-2, Q&A-5. Remember that once a small business surpasses ten employees, the exemption permanently terminates. 
 Review Plan Mergers and Acquisition Agreements: In corporate mergers and acquisitions, ensure that any pre-enactment grandfathered plan is affirmatively designated as the ongoing plan in writing, and that the merger is formally executed within the statutory transition period under Code Section 410(b)(6)(C)(ii). 
 Implement Universal EACA Deferral and Escalation Engines: Ensure recordkeeping platforms are configured to cover all eligible employees—including collectively bargained and LTPT employees—who do not have an affirmative election in effect. Configure escalation rules to ensure default rates increase by at least 1 percentage point no later than the first day of each plan year following the initial period, capping default escalation between 10 percent and 15 percent. 
 Incorporate Permissible Withdrawal Features: Confirm that plan documents and administrative procedures afford defaulted participants a 90-day window following the initial default deferral to elect a permissible withdrawal under Code Section 414(w)(2) without incurring the 10 percent early distribution tax under Code Section 72(t).
